source.title: Test-Time Unlearning via Sparse Autoencoder
source.authors: Ping-Zhi Li; Jinhao Duan; Vaishnav Tadiparthi; Nakul Agarwal; Kwonjoon Lee; E. Pari; Hossein Nourkhiz Mahjoub; Si-Jia Liu; Tianlong Chen

record.file_problem: Whole paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests post-unlearning recovery attacks using a different, test-time unlearning method, ARIA, and reports the effects on targeted WMDP-cyber accuracy and MMLU.
record.gate_note: The paper reports cited prior findings about weight-based unlearning attacks, but those cited results are not rows. It measures clean ARIA and weight-based baseline performance, and applies repeated-sampling, prompt, and continued-SFT attacks to ARIA. It does not apply those attacks to the weight-based baselines.
record.test_reason: The study proposes ARIA, a test-time SAE-gated refusal method that leaves weights frozen. It reports ARIA's resistance to repeated sampling, prompt rewrites and continued SFT on WMDP-cyber, which bears on version F. It also reports clean, unattacked results for four weight-based baselines (GA, GD, NPO, RMU), which bear only on the first half of version A. No attack is applied to any weight-unlearned model, so B, C, D and E are not tested for the systems those versions describe.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct, with two additions. The authors claim ARIA beats weight-based baselines on the forget-retain trade-off across TOFU, R-TOFU and WMDP-cyber, with negligible inference overhead. They also acknowledge ARIA is access control rather than weight removal, so white-box access can bypass it by removing the detector.
record.recipe_differences: ARIA leaves the base model weights frozen and applies detector-gated test-time intervention using SAE features, rather than using a global weight edit such as gradient ascent, NPO, or RMU. The paper evaluates the latter as clean baselines but attacks ARIA.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports a forget-retain trade-off as the ARIA detector threshold changes: lower thresholds improve forgetting while higher thresholds preserve more retain utility. Attack results also vary by attack type and model.

fits_no_version.finding: SAE attribution traces retain false positives to response-style latents (e.g., assertive answer openings) common in the WMDP-cyber forget set, not to cyber knowledge.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Unlearning benchmarks' forget sets carry stylistic artifacts that detectors or unlearning methods can latch onto, conflating style with knowledge.

record.problems: The attack experiments cover two open-weight models and WMDP-cyber only. The continued-SFT training data and amount are not stated. Prompt attack variants are reported as a family, without separate scores. No uncertainty estimates are given. The study does not test quantization or activation-direction ablation.

untested.parts: Whether simple attacks recover knowledge from the weight-based baselines; they are evaluated clean only.
Not tested: no fine-tuning attack is applied to any weight-unlearned model.
Not tested on weight-unlearned models; prompt attacks are applied only to ARIA.

Quantization, activation-direction ablation, adaptive attacks on the detector, and white-box removal of the detector. The continued-SFT data, size and steps are unstated. Only WMDP-cyber on two ~1B models is covered.

missing.what: TOFU and R-TOFU results for ARIA and the baselines (e.g., R-TOFU AFE/CFE: ARIA 97.45/97.24 vs RMU 73.02/74.54; TOFU Forget Quality 0.01% for ARIA).
Detector-threshold scaling trade-off between forgetting and MMLU on Gemma for WMDP-cyber.
Authors' statement that white-box access bypasses ARIA by removing the detector.

record.verdict_notes: ARIA blocks access at inference; it does not delete knowledge from the weights. Its robustness bears on F, not on whether weight unlearning is shallow (B–E), so the reader's B and E 'challenges' labels are dropped. ARIA's 0.00% exact-match is a refusal ('I don't know'), below the ~25% chance level of 4-way MC. Pre-unlearning WMDP-cyber accuracy is only ~32%, about 7 points above chance, so the baseline comparison has little headroom. No uncertainty is reported, and continued-SFT details are absent.

versions.untested_parts: The attack evaluation is on ARIA only, not the weight-based baselines. The study does not test whether ARIA's results hold on models or datasets beyond those reported.

The continued-SFT attack is tested, but its training-set size, relation to the forgotten facts, and training details are not stated. The study does not establish results for small unrelated, loosely related, or forgotten-fact subsets separately.
No activation-direction ablation or analysis showing that weight-based methods block access rather than delete knowledge is tested.
Quantization of unlearned weights is not tested.
Prompt rewrites and in-context examples are tested, but jailbreaks and other-language prompts are not reported.
ARIA is tested against repeated sampling, prompt attacks, and continued SFT. It is not tested against activation edits or quantization, and the continued-SFT recipe is not specified.

source_check.notes: All three attacks (Leak@K, prompt rewrites, continued SFT with unstated data/size) run only on ARIA; the GA/GD/NPO/RMU baselines are evaluated clean only. ARIA's 0.00% comes from forced 'I don't know' answers under generative exact match. Pre-unlearning WMDP-cyber accuracy is only about 32%, little above 25% chance. Table 3 parentheses are changes vs clean ARIA, so the 0.45 MMLU figure leaves out clean ARIA's own cost (-0.50 DeepSeek, -1.36 Gemma).

statements.correction: ARIA on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B: repeated sampling (Leak@16, Leak@64), a prompt-rewrite family and continued SFT (Table 3, Appendix C). No quantization or activation-direction ablation is run.
statements.problem: Says ARIA on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B faced only prompts and continued SFT. It also faced the repeated-sampling attack (Leak@16/64).
